functions.description: Echo service loop: reads up to 256 bytes into 112-byte stack buffer, echoes via printf('%s'), asks Y/N to continue. Loop exits on Y/y. Canary protected.

attack_surfaces.operation: WRITE to stack buffer of 112 bytes with 256-byte read
attack_surfaces.reason: read() writes up to 0x100(256) bytes into a buffer at rbp-0x70 which is only 0x70(112) bytes. The canary is at rbp-0x8 (0x68 bytes from buffer start), saved rbp at rbp+0 (0x70 bytes), return address at rbp+0x8 (0x78 bytes). With 256 bytes of input, attacker can overwrite canary, saved rbp, and return address. This is a classic stack buffer overflow.

attack_surfaces.operation: READ unbounded string from stack buffer for echo output
attack_surfaces.reason: printf uses %s format on the stack buffer. The newline-to-NUL replacement only triggers if the byte at buf[read_retval] is 0x0a. If the attacker sends exactly N bytes without a trailing newline (or fills the buffer completely), the buffer may not be null-terminated, causing printf to read past the 112-byte buffer boundary and leak stack data including the canary value. This is a potential info leak that could bypass the stack canary protection.

attack_surfaces.operation: WRITE up to 7 chars to continue_flag at rbp-0x78
attack_surfaces.reason: scanf %7s writes at most 7 chars to rbp-0x78 which is 8 bytes above the echo buffer at rbp-0x70. The 7-char limit plus null terminator fits in 8 bytes. Low risk but adjacent to the echo buffer.
